query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy or refractory high‐entropy alloys, introducing oxidation‐resistant elements (such as Cr, and in some cases combined with Si in a coating) enhances oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an alloy rich in Ni, Co, Fe with added elements for strengthening) that in its standard composition shows moderate oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Addition of oxidation‐resistant elements (by alloying Cr into the bulk or applying a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating via a fused slurry method) to promote protective oxide scale formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidative environments (typically above 800 °C) where the formation and stability of protective oxides (e.g., Cr2O3 or silicide-derived oxides) are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense protective oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3, or silicide-derived oxides) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The oxidation-resistant elements react at elevated temperatures with oxygen to form adherent oxide scales that act as diffusion barriers, reducing both the inward oxygen flux and the outward diffusion of metal species, thereby slowing the overall oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Lower oxidation weight gain and reduced degradation at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy without the additional oxidation‐resistant elements or coating.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or untreated high-entropy alloy composition that exhibits higher oxidation rates due to less effective oxide scale formation.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be beneficial primarily under high-temperature conditions where the protective oxide scale remains stable; its efficacy may be limited by processing details or in environments where the oxide scale spalls off.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., degree of reduction in oxidation kinetics) may vary with alloy composition, coating uniformity, and specific test conditions. Quantitative performance differences need to be established through controlled experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with the added oxidation-resistant elements (or with a applied Si-20Cr-20Fe coating) and one control set without these modifications. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere) for a fixed duration.
measurements: Mass gain measurements to determine the oxidation rate
Surface and cross-sectional analysis via SEM/EDS
XRD analysis to identify the formation and continuity of oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate (i.e., mass gain) or fail to form a continuous, protective oxide layer compared to the control samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that the intervention improves oxidation resistance is falsified.

MoNbTaTiW RHEA with an equimolar ratio of the elements was prepared by spark plasma sintering. Commercially available Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and W elemental powders were used as raw materials. The purity of all the powders was higher than 99.5%. The particle size of Mo, Nb, Ta, and Ti were less than 38 µm and that of W was less than 5 µm. After being proportioned in an equal molar ratio, the powders were mixed by planetary ball milling for 6 h. The mixed powders were put into a graphite mold and sintered in a spark plasma sintering furnace by vacuum hot pressing. The sintering temperature was 1500 °C, the pressure was 30 MPa, and the holding time was 20 min. The as-prepared MoNbTaTiW RHEA was used as the substrates. The MoNbTaTiW RHEA was cut into 5 mm × 5 mm × 20 mm cuboids whose surfaces were polished using 2000 mesh sandpaper and cleaned with acetone.

A Si-20Cr-20Fe (wt.%) coating was prepared on the RHEA cuboids by a fused slurry method. The particle size of Si powder was less than 10 µm, and that of Cr powder and Fe powder was less than 76 µm.
